section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Bernoulli Trial
section_1.content: Define the building block: a Bernoulli trial. Emphasize three requirements: only two outcomes (Success/Failure), constant probability (p), and independent trials. Visual: A light switch flipping between On (Success) and Off (Failure).
section_1.example: Flipping a fair coin: Head (Success, p=0.5) or Tail (Failure, q=0.5).

section_2.title: Defining the Binomial Setup
section_2.content: Introduce the Binomial Distribution as a sequence of 'n' independent Bernoulli trials. Define the random variable X as the total number of successes. Visual: A sequence of n slots filling with either 'S' or 'F'.
section_2.example: A robot dog tries to jump through 5 hoops. Each attempt has a 70% success rate. X is the total number of hoops successfully cleared.

section_3.title: The Binomial Formula Breakdown
section_3.content: Deconstruct the formula P(X=k) = C(n,k) * p^k * (1-p)^(n-k). Explain the 'n choose k' (combinations) as the number of ways to arrange successes, and the probability product as the likelihood of that specific sequence. Visual: Animated tree diagram collapsing into the formula components.
section_3.example: Calculating the probability that the robot dog clears exactly 3 out of 5 hoops: C(5,3) * (0.7)^3 * (0.3)^2.

section_4.title: Visualizing the Probability Mass Function
section_4.content: Explain how the distribution changes based on 'n' and 'p'. Show a bar chart transforming as 'p' shifts from 0.1 to 0.5 to 0.9. Emphasize that the sum of all probabilities equals 1. Visual: A dynamic histogram shifting shape.
section_4.example: Comparing the robot dog's success probability (p=0.7) vs. a 'lucky' cat's jump probability (p=0.2) over 10 trials.

section_5.title: Application & Wrap-up
section_5.content: Summarize real-world use cases (Quality control, genetics, risk assessment). Recap that the Binomial distribution is essential for predicting outcomes in fixed-trial experiments. Visual: Icon cluster showing a factory line, DNA strands, and dice.
section_5.example: A quality control device checking 100 microchips; using binomial distribution to find the probability of having 0 defective chips.
